clinicalPearls: Starts as a tender pustule or nodule that rapidly breaks down into an ulcer with a violaceous, undermined, overhanging border
Classic feature is pathergy — new or worsening ulceration at sites of minor trauma, injection, or surgical incision
About half of cases are associated with an underlying systemic disease, most commonly inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or a hematologic malignancy/paraproteinemia
Diagnosis is one of exclusion; there is no single confirmatory laboratory or histologic test
Ulcer base often shows purulent, necrotic tissue with a boggy, undermined edge rather than a clean granulating base
Lower extremities (especially pretibial region) are the most common site, but PG can occur anywhere including peristomal skin
Debridement and skin grafting can worsen lesions via pathergy and should generally be avoided until disease activity is controlled
Response to immunosuppressive therapy, when it occurs, supports the diagnosis retrospectively
harrison.pathophysiology: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis thought to arise from dysregulated innate immune activation and neutrophil chemotaxis/function, often in a genetically predisposed host. Cytokine-driven neutrophilic infiltration in the skin, without a demonstrable infectious trigger, produces sterile abscess-like tissue destruction. The tendency for lesions to develop at sites of trauma (pathergy) reflects this exaggerated local inflammatory response. Its frequent association with inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritides, and myeloid dyscrasias suggests a shared systemic inflammatory or clonal process in many patients.
additionalDifferentials: Necrotizing fasciitis or other necrotizing soft-tissue infection
Cutaneous malignancy (e.g., ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma)
Brown recluse spider bite / factitial ulceration
infectionMimics: Deep fungal or atypical mycobacterial ulcer
Cutaneous anthrax or other bacterial ulcerative infection
nonInfectiousMimics: Venous stasis or arterial insufficiency ulcer
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histology and tissue culture — helps exclude infection and vasculitis, though PG findings are nonspecific
Tissue and blood cultures — to rule out an infectious ulcer before immunosuppression is started
Complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear — screens for underlying myeloproliferative or myelodysplastic disease
Serum protein electrophoresis/immunofixation — evaluates for paraproteinemia associated with PG
Colonoscopy or evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease — assesses for a common associated condition
ANCA, rheumatoid factor, and autoimmune serologies — helps exclude vasculitis and screens for associated rheumatologic disease
Ankle-brachial index or vascular studies — excludes arterial/venous insufficiency contributing to ulceration
Coagulation/hypercoagulability workup if calciphylaxis or thrombotic ulcer is a concern
redFlags: Rapidly expanding ulcer with systemic toxicity — reconsider necrotizing infection and seek urgent surgical/infectious disease input
Worsening of the ulcer after debridement or grafting, consistent with pathergy, warrants stopping surgical intervention and escalating immunosuppression
New PG lesions in a patient with known IBD may signal a disease flare requiring gastroenterology involvement
Unexplained cytopenias or monoclonal gammopathy alongside PG should prompt hematologic evaluation for underlying malignancy
Peristomal PG in patients with ostomies can be mistaken for a wound infection and mismanaged
pitfalls: Treating PG as an infected wound and pursuing aggressive debridement, which can worsen the ulcer through pathergy
Assuming a positive wound culture confirms infection rather than colonization of a chronic ulcer
Delaying diagnosis by relying on a single confirmatory test rather than the clinical picture and exclusion of mimics
Missing an underlying systemic disease (IBD, arthritis, hematologic disorder) that drives disease activity and recurrence risk
harrison.prognosis: Course is variable and often relapsing, particularly when an underlying systemic disease remains active; lesions can heal with characteristic cribriform (atrophic, often hyperpigmented) scarring. Prompt recognition, avoidance of unnecessary surgical intervention, and treatment of any associated systemic condition improve outcomes.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Cutaneous Manifestations of Internal Disease / Neutrophilic Dermatoses
management: Induce remission with systemic immunosuppression, using high-potency corticosteroids as first line and ciclosporin as an alternative or steroid-sparing agent
Escalate refractory or inflammatory-bowel-disease-associated disease to TNF-alpha inhibitors such as infliximab or adalimumab
Treat localised disease with potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids or a topical calcineurin inhibitor such as tacrolimus
Provide meticulous moist wound care with non-adherent dressings and adequate analgesia, avoiding aggressive surgical debridement or unnecessary grafting because of pathergy
Protect the skin from trauma, injections and surgery at new sites to prevent pathergy-induced ulceration
Identify and treat any associated condition, most often inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis or a haematological or myeloproliferative disorder
Coordinate care across dermatology with gastroenterology, rheumatology or haematology as dictated by the underlying association
